title: LRU Cache
followUps: Walk me through why each operation is O(1). Which data structure provides which guarantee?
How would you make this cache safe to use from multiple threads? What would the lock granularity be?
How would you add per-entry TTL (time-based expiry) on top of LRU eviction?
If this cache were distributed across several machines, how would you decide which node owns a key, and what happens when a node is added?

interviewer.approach: Hash map from key to node in a doubly linked list ordered by recency (head = most recent). get: look up, move to head. put: update/insert at head, evict tail when over capacity. Both O(1). Languages with insertion-ordered maps (Python OrderedDict/dict, JS Map) allow a compact solution: delete and reinsert to refresh recency, and evict the first key. Accept either, but in strict settings ask whether they could implement it without the built-in ordered map.
hints: You need O(1) lookup by key and O(1) tracking of usage order. Can a single structure do both, or do you need two?
A hash map gives fast lookup. What structure lets you move an arbitrary element to the front and remove from the back in O(1)?
Store doubly-linked-list nodes in the map. Sentinel head and tail nodes simplify the edge cases.
pitfalls: Forgetting that get() also refreshes recency.
Updating an existing key without refreshing its recency, or evicting when updating an existing key.
Evicting the most recent instead of the least recent.
O(n) list scans (e.g. list.remove) that break the O(1) requirement.
